title: Learning Generalizable Hand-Object Tracking Control without Human Demonstrations
claim: A synthetic data generator feeds a teacher-student RL tracker, which converts diverse high-level inputs into controllable, trackable manipulation behavior.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, large arrows between, colored pastel backgrounds per stage
description: Three pastel-tinted panels read left to right, linked by bold block arrows. (a) green panel: dice icon and 'Traj Params' feed a green HOG box, which outputs a 'Large-Scale Synthetic HOI Traj' card showing a 3x3 grid of rendered hands manipulating a Rubik's cube, a tool and a bottle along dotted trajectory curves. (b) yellow panel: stacked red HOT-teacher network, a Simulator globe, and a blue HOT-student network, with circular arrows, a 'Behavior Clone' gradient pill, yellow stacked 'Refined Traj' cards and a dotted 'HOI Imitation Reward' feedback loop. (c) blue panel: inputs (LLM/VLM, generative model, human demonstration) merge into Traj Params, then HOG, HOT, and a 'Target Manipulation' strip showing a hand moving a knife onto a block.
caption: Our system learns generalizable hand-object tracking from synthetic data. (a) HOG synthesizes manipulation trajectories for meta-skills. (b) HOT is trained through a two-stage teacherstudent framework using reinforcement learning with a unified HOI imitation reward, enabling robust tracking of the target HOI trajectories. (c) At inference, the system can accept high-level waypoints from language models, generative models, or human data, which HOG converts into trajectories for HOT to track, enabling diverse applications.
abstract: We present a system for learning generalizable hand-object tracking controllers purely from synthetic data, without requiring any human demonstrations. Our approach makes two key contributions: (1) HOG, a highly efficient Hand-Object data generator that rapidly synthesizes diverse, large-scale, and uniformly distributed trajectories; and (2) HOT, a Hand-Object Tracker that bridges synthetic-to-physical transfer through reinforcement learning and interaction imitation learning. Our method extends to diverse object shapes and hand morphologies. HOT also enables cross-simulator transfer. Through extensive evaluations, we show that our approach enables dexterous hands to track challenging, long-horizon sequences including object re-arrangement and agile in-hand reorientation. These results represent a significant step toward scalable foundation controllers for manipulation that can learn entirely from simple, scalable synthetic data, breaking the data bottleneck that has long constrained progress in dexterous manipulation.
